items.summary: PCE inflation data for May 2026 has been released. Headline PCE came in at 4.1% annual rate — the highest since April 2023 and meaningfully above the Federal Reserve's 2% target — with a monthly gain of +0.4%. The annual figure is above Chair Warsh's June Summary of Economic Projections projection of 3.6%, the most consequential single-figure gap in the current Fed watch. The monthly print of +0.4% came in softer than the Wells Fargo forecast of +0.5%, removing the acute upside surprise scenario while confirming the persistent elevated baseline. Core PCE (excluding food and energy) printed at 3.4% annual and +0.3% MoM, also above the 3.3% SEP projection. Personal consumption expenditures rose 0.7% for the month; personal income rose 0.7% — a simultaneously buoyant consumer and elevated-price read that constitutes the textbook stagflationary data signature. The implications for the Fed: the nine FOMC members who projected at least one 2026 hike in the June SEP now have the PCE annual print confirming their underlying thesis — energy-cost passthrough from the Hormuz closure period has embedded in consumption prices with a lag, and the Warsh hold at 3.50-3.75% is under sustained upward pressure. The ECB and Bank of Japan tightening posture, plus the Bank Indonesia 25bp hike to 5.75% this cycle, frame the global synchronized tightening backdrop. The softer monthly read reduces the probability of an emergency July inter-meeting discussion but does not eliminate the September hike scenario that nine dots have already penciled in. For markets: the mixed signal — annual rate above SEP, monthly below forecast — is likely to produce a modestly risk-positive open. WTI holds at approximately $73.7 for a fourth consecutive session below the $74 normalization-confidence floor. The pump relief chain remains gated on the SNSC determination and downstream Lloyd's normalization: Iran retraction → Lloyd's announcement → 118-tanker backlog release → WTI $65-70 supply pulse → pump relief. Oregon gas approximately $5.35/gallon; national approximately $4.56/gallon.

items.summary: Friday June 26 is the next anticipated SCOTUS opinion day for the remaining term-end cases, with Trump v. Barbara (birthright citizenship, EO 14160) and Watson v. RNC (mail ballot counting) the two most consequential outstanding decisions. Both have been pending since April 1, 2026 oral arguments. The Court's end-of-June-term pattern produces consecutive opinion days in the final week; with the term expected to close in late June or early July, Friday is among the highest-probability remaining opinion windows. Trump v. Barbara tests EO 14160's constitutionality against the 14th Amendment citizenship clause. Every lower court has found the EO violates the 14th Amendment. April 1 oral argument questioning was described as 'icy' toward the government's position — a signal often correlating with adverse rulings, though not determinative at the Supreme Court level. The 6-3 conservative supermajority creates irreducible outcome uncertainty. Watson v. RNC determines the mechanics of mail-ballot counting for November 2026 — which states can count ballots postmarked by Election Day but received after. Whichever way it lands, it reshapes state election administration planning with under five months to November 2026 midterms. Louisiana v. Callais (issued June 23, 6-3) remains operative on Day 4: the Alabama discriminatory congressional map is deployed for 2026 elections, the Section 2 VRA evidentiary bar has been substantially raised, and Senate Democrats under Schumer continue exploring a new VRA legislative pathway with uncertain prospects in the 119th Congress. Trump administration expedited deportation operations continue active following the Tuesday federal appeals court authorization; ICE/CBP deployment infrastructure operationalizing under Secure America Act Day 14. Reconciliation 2.0 at T-3 Rules: Friday is the final practical pre-deadline scheduling window.
